risks.title: Single database with no replica or backup configuration
risks.why: The model has one database and none of the files read mention a replica, a standby, a backup tool or a managed database service.
risks.check: Confirm where backups are taken and that a restore has been tried. Decide whether a replica or a managed service is worth its cost for this project.

fixes.text: Take scheduled backups and rehearse a restore.
fixes.tradeoff: Costs storage and an hour of practice; it protects against loss, not against downtime.

fixes.text: Use a managed database that handles backups and failover.
fixes.tradeoff: Less control and a monthly bill; fewer things to run yourself.

fixes.text: Add a read replica or standby.
fixes.tradeoff: Costs money and adds replication lag; a replica is not a backup.

risks.title: Cache entries written without an expiry
risks.why: Heuristic: a Redis write has no expiry option (EX, PX, ttl) and no expire call close by, so the entry stays until it is evicted or deleted.
risks.check: Check the eviction policy and whether these keys should expire. Some data (counters, locks you release yourself) is meant to stay; adding a TTL there can lose data.

fixes.text: Set an expiry (EX, PX or ttl) when the entry can be rebuilt.
fixes.tradeoff: A short expiry means more cache misses and more load on the source.

fixes.text: Set a memory limit and an eviction policy on Redis.
fixes.tradeoff: Entries can disappear when memory is full, so keep only data you can rebuild.

risks.title: No rate limiting found on a public API
risks.why: Heuristic: the app defines public routes (including Next.js route handlers), but no rate-limit package, middleware or helper appears in the dependencies or code read. It may be done at a gateway, CDN or proxy that these files do not show.
risks.check: Look for rate limiting at the proxy, CDN or API gateway. If there is none, consider limits on login, signup and expensive routes first.

fixes.text: Add a rate limiter at the proxy, CDN or gateway.
fixes.tradeoff: One place to manage; the app itself stays unaware of limits.

fixes.text: Add a limiter in the app, first on login, signup and expensive routes.
fixes.tradeoff: Needs a shared store such as Redis to work across instances; users behind one address share a limit.

risks.title: External call without a timeout

evidence.note: fetch to api.stripe.com without a timeout

risks.why: Heuristic: a call to an outside host has no AbortSignal.timeout, signal or timeout option, so a slow provider can hold the request open.
risks.check: Check the client's default timeout. Add an explicit one that is shorter than your own request limit, and decide what the user sees when it fires.

fixes.text: Set a timeout on the call or on the shared client, shorter than your own request limit.
fixes.tradeoff: A timeout that is too short cuts off slow successes.

fixes.text: Pair the timeout with one retry and a clear error for the user.
fixes.tradeoff: Retries multiply load on a provider that is already slow.

risks.title: Database query inside a loop

evidence.note: awaited database call inside a loop

risks.why: Heuristic: an awaited database call sits inside a loop or an async map, which often means one query per item (the N+1 pattern).
risks.check: Check how many items the loop runs over. A single batched query (findMany with a list, a join, an IN clause) is usually faster, but can be heavier for very large lists.

fixes.text: Load the items with one batched query (a list, a join, an IN clause).
fixes.tradeoff: Can use more memory or hit parameter limits on very large lists.

fixes.text: Keep the loop but cap the number of items.
fixes.tradeoff: Simple, but later items are skipped or need paging.

risks.title: Secret-looking variable exposed to the browser
risks.why: A variable with a browser-exposed prefix (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_ and similar) has a name containing SECRET, PRIVATE, KEY, TOKEN or PASSWORD. Such variables are copied into the public JavaScript bundle. Only the name was read, never the value.
risks.check: Check whether the value is really meant to be public. If it is a secret, move it to the server and rotate it, because it may already be in a deployed bundle.

fixes.text: Move the value to the server and call it from there.
fixes.tradeoff: One more request hop for the browser.

fixes.text: If it was a secret, rotate it, because it may already be in a deployed bundle.
fixes.tradeoff: Anything using the old value must be updated.

risks.title: No health check endpoint found
risks.why: Heuristic: the app defines routes but none of the files read has a /health, /healthz or /ready route.
risks.check: Check whether your host, load balancer or orchestrator probes the service another way (a TCP check, the home page). If not, a small health route lets it restart or stop sending traffic to a stuck instance.

fixes.text: Add a small liveness route that returns 200 without touching other services.
fixes.tradeoff: Cheap, but it only shows the process is up.

fixes.text: Add a separate readiness route that checks the database.
fixes.tradeoff: A slow database can then take the instance out of rotation; keep it apart from liveness.

risks.title: Data service exposed or unprotected in docker-compose

evidence.note: db: port 5432:5432 published on all interfaces
cache: port 6379:6379 published on all interfaces
cache: Redis has no requirepass or REDIS_PASSWORD

risks.why: A compose service for a data store publishes its port to the host on all interfaces, or Redis has no password (requirepass) configured.
risks.check: Check where this compose file is used. For local development it is often fine; on a shared or public machine, bind ports to 127.0.0.1, set a password and keep the service off public networks.

fixes.text: Bind published ports to 127.0.0.1 or remove them.
fixes.tradeoff: Other machines can no longer reach the service, including ones that should.

fixes.text: Set a password (requirepass) and keep the service off public networks.
fixes.tradeoff: Every client needs the password.

risks.title: Some synchronous calls have a timeout recorded and these do not
risks.why: Heuristic: the model records a timeout on at least one synchronous connection but not on these, so the calls may behave differently when a service is slow. A model that records no timeouts at all is not flagged, because that only means none were looked for.
risks.check: Look at the client or call behind each connection. Decide whether the missing timeout is deliberate, and record it in the model when it is set.

fixes.text: Set an explicit timeout on each call, shorter than your own request limit.
fixes.tradeoff: A timeout that is too short cuts off slow successes.

fixes.text: Share one client configuration so every call gets the same timeout.
fixes.tradeoff: One value fits all calls badly if some are slower on purpose.

risks.title: Retries with no backoff noted
risks.why: Heuristic: a connection retries a failed call, and nothing in its evidence notes a delay between attempts (backoff or jitter). Immediate retries can pile load onto a service that is already struggling.
risks.check: Check how the retry waits. If it retries at once, add a growing delay with some randomness, and a limit on attempts.

fixes.text: Wait longer after each failed attempt (exponential backoff) and add jitter.
fixes.tradeoff: Slower recovery for the caller when the failure was brief.

fixes.text: Cap the number of attempts and fail with a clear error.
fixes.tradeoff: Some calls that would have succeeded on a later try now fail.

risks.title: Connection crosses a trust zone with no authentication or encryption

evidence.note: agent-mcp: crosses private to third-party with no authentication

risks.why: A connection joins components in different trust zones and is recorded as having no authentication (auth: none) or no TLS (tls: false), with a file as evidence.
risks.check: Check whether the connection stays on a private network that you control. If it can be reached from outside its zone, add authentication and encryption.

fixes.text: Turn on TLS for the connection (mutual TLS inside a private network if you can).
fixes.tradeoff: Certificates to issue and renew; a small cost per connection.

fixes.text: Require a credential (a token, API key or signed request) on the receiving side.
fixes.tradeoff: Every caller needs the credential and a way to rotate it.

risks.title: Personal data reaches a third party or logs
risks.why: A connection is recorded as carrying personal data (pii) to a component in the third-party zone or to one that holds logs, or a third-party component is recorded as holding it.
risks.check: Check whether this data really goes there, what the other side does with it, and whether it can be left out, masked or hashed first.

fixes.text: Remove or mask personal fields before the data leaves (or before it is logged).
fixes.tradeoff: Support and debugging lose some detail.

fixes.text: Check the third party's data agreement and retention, and record the decision.
fixes.tradeoff: Takes time; it may show the service is not a fit.

risks.title: Single copy of a component that several flows depend on

evidence.note: api: one replica, used by 3 flows

risks.why: A component is recorded as running as one replica, and three or more request flows pass through it, so one failure or restart interrupts all of them.
risks.check: Check whether one copy is enough: how long a restart takes, and what the flows do while it is gone.

fixes.text: Run a second copy behind a load balancer.
fixes.tradeoff: Costs more, and state held in memory must move out or be shared.

fixes.text: Keep one copy but add a health check and fast automatic restart.
fixes.tradeoff: There is still a gap during each restart.
